Explanation shelf, read whole (verified): Puranam, Alexy and Reitzig (2014). Its claims that bear here: a form of organizing is a set of solutions to four universal problems, individually necessary and collectively sufficient (p. 166); goalless networks and crowds are ruled out (p. 164); self-selection, transparent task division, intrinsic reward and virtual collaboration are complements (pp. 173-174); visible work simplifies coordination (p. 172); authority in open source is the right to accept or reject contributions and membership (p. 173). First reading: it is the standing claim for C3c, and it resembles more than it contradicts (visible work, a host's right to accept guests). Next: Felin and Zenger (2017).

Explanation shelf, read whole (verified): Felin and Zenger (2017). Claims that bear here: economic actors' theories (questions, problems, contrarian beliefs) direct perception and reveal value (pp. 260-263); organizations grant some actors' theories power, aid their composition, and attract those who share the theory by self-selection (p. 265); hierarchy decides when discussion does not (Simon, quoted p. 265). First reading: a candidate contradiction on what settles what a room acts on (a chosen theory against the topic's given picture), and a resemblance in self-selection to a starter's proposal. Next: Felin and Zenger (2016).

Explanation shelf, read whole (verified): Felin and Zenger (2016, SSRN manuscript pages). Claims that bear here: a firm's theory reveals an architecture and bundle of problems to solve, and guides which to solve itself and which to leave to others (pp. 4-5, 11); serendipitous need-solution pairs are others' priced solutions (p. 8); even recognizing a solution needs a theory (p. 14). First reading: with the 2017 paper, a candidate contradiction on what settles a room's work; the room's goal (a picture) is mostly given, not composed as a contrarian theory. Next: O'Mahony and Ferraro (2007).

Explanation shelf, read whole (verified): O'Mahony and Ferraro (2007). Claims that bear here: 'Before an organization can develop a form of governance, it must establish a shared basis of authority' (p. 1081); Debian ran five years on de facto founder rule, recalled an autocratic second leader, then wrote a constitution with positional authority limited by democratic means (pp. 1088-1090); members came to elect organization builders, and face-to-face ties predicted the leadership team (pp. 1091, 1098). First reading: a contradiction with the model's claim that rooms organized almost without decided order; the likely resolution is the setting (73 hours against 13 years), to be decided from the record. Next: Bechky (2006).

Explanation shelf, read whole (verified): Bechky (2006). Claims that bear here: temporary organizations are not ephemeral but 'organized around structured role systems whose nuances are negotiated in situ' (p. 3); the generalized role structure travels by interorganizational careers, and film sets are temporary total institutions (pp. 8-10); roles are enacted by enthusiastic thanking, polite admonishing and role-oriented joking (pp. 11-13); she asks 'how temporary organizing can be successful in settings without a generalized role structure' (p. 17). First reading: a contradiction about what coordinates a temporary group (a carried role structure against calls and a visible work), likely resolved as a difference of setting the paper itself names; the enactment practices resemble the rooms' credit and refusals. Next: March (1991).

Explanation shelf, read whole (verified): March (1991), read last and weighted below the others. Claims that bear here: an organizational code that newcomers learn and that learns from them (mutual learning, pp. 74-75); slow socialization and moderate turnover keep the diversity the code learns from, 'the development of knowledge may depend on maintaining an influx of the naive and ignorant' (p. 86); exploitation crowds out exploration (p. 73). First reading: no contradiction with the model; a resemblance for C3b on newcomers and the host sub's code. All six works of the read tier are read. Next: the contradictions, with the model's statements on roles and decided order.

Abductive read, prompted by O'Mahony and Ferraro (2007): a production community establishes a shared basis of authority before it can govern itself (p. 1081), and the canvas-born factions at the far end of the decided-order claim's range look like that. What it makes me look for: whether decided order (rooms placed on Decided order) gathers in rooms that rule on other rooms' works (hosts vetting guests' requests, T3-162; colour factions, Neo-tribes T4-023) more than in other rooms, held to room size by items_in_window quartile with a permutation null within quartile (seed 20261014), counted with mem.py rooms --with over the 705 analysed rooms; then quotes through cite.py from the rooms that show it. A rooms --with T4-011 call with --limit 5 was run before this line to see the output format; it served four room names.

Move (relating or contrasting), abductive, prompted by O'Mahony and Ferraro (2007): F-006 (decided order is rare) superseded by a bounded line, and a C01 history line written (abductive, prompted_by). Decided order gathers in rooms placed on a colour-faction theme or on vetting guests' requests: 7 of 39 (0.179) against 39 of 666 (0.059); held to size 7 against a null mean of 2.7 (p95 5, p 0.014); the gap is in the two smaller size quartiles (5 of 14 against 13 of 339) and vanishes in the two larger (2 of 25 against 26 of 327); 0 of 56 rooms that asked a host for space. The disagreement is about the setting (73 hours and one picture against 13 years and one code base) and bounds the claim. findings.jsonl 21 lines, history.jsonl 83. Snapped C3-move-relating-48. Abductive read, prompted by conversation analysis (recalled: Schegloff and Sacks 1973 on adjacency pairs; Pomerantz 1984 and Levinson 1983 on preference organization): a call is a first pair part, an acceptance its preferred second, a refusal its dispreferred second; dispreferred seconds come marked, with accounts. What it makes me look for: replies to attack moves in the same thread (out/_analysis/c3b_ca_pairs.py, mem.py codes --fourth T4-020 and T4-015 --json), one earliest acceptance (a reply under T4-020) and one earliest refusal (a reply under T4-015) per room, a seeded sample of up to 40 rooms each (seed 20261014), read whole. Rules written before reading: a pair counts only if its first part, read whole, calls for or proposes an attack; others are set aside and counted. An account is a clause in the reply giving a reason or ground for its stance: a because, since or so clause; a stated rule or norm; a fact offered as a ground (allies, first there, their flag); a consequence. A bare assent, a bare refusal, a directive with no ground, a joke or a report of action is not an account. Prediction: refusals carry an account more often than acceptances and are longer. It fails if the shares are about equal.

Result of the conversation-analysis read (c3b_ca_tally.txt): of 80 seeded pairs, 57 had a first part that calls for or proposes an attack. By read stance, refusals gave an account in 23 of 38 (0.61) and acceptances in 2 of 14 (0.14), one-sided Fisher p 0.003. The length half of the prediction fails: median reply words 9.5 for refusals against 11.5 for acceptances, since acceptances carry tactics and coordinates. The theme a reply sits under does not track its stance (18 of 33 under restraint, 9 of 24 under contention). Coded by the analyst alone.

Abductive read, prompted by threshold models of collective behaviour (recalled: Granovetter 1978, people act once enough others have, and must see how many have): the concept claims a room with no roster reads its numbers off the one-line replies under a call. What it makes me look for: in turns placed on the doubt-about-numbers element's theme (T4-012, Collective efficacy), a seeded sample of up to 40 rooms' first such turn (seed 20261014), read whole, on what each judgment of numbers rests. Rules written before reading: a turn counts only if it judges the room's own hands or numbers (too few, enough, how many). Its ground is 'thread' if it cites who answered or is present (replies, people here, joiners, silence), 'canvas' if it cites the work's state on the canvas (overrun, losing pixels, not growing), 'both', or 'none' if it gives no ground. Prediction: 'thread' or 'both' in a clear share. It fails if judgments of numbers rest almost only on the canvas.

Result of the threshold-model read (c3b_threshold_codes.json): of 40 seeded first turns on the doubt-about-numbers theme (726 concepts in 89 rooms), 11 judge the room's own hands. None of the 11 rests on who answered or is present in the thread: 4 rest on the readership's size (a ground not foreseen in the rules, coded apart), 2 on the canvas, 1 on both readership and canvas, 4 on nothing. The prediction fails. A thread ground does appear outside the sample ('I mean I want to but nobody's here', torontoraptors c0060, in the conversation-analysis sample). Weak: one theme, one coder, an absence claim. It weakens the concept's claim that a room reads its numbers off the one-line replies.

Move (relating or contrasting), section 4a, abductive, prompted by conversation analysis (recalled: Schegloff and Sacks 1973; Pomerantz 1984; Levinson 1983): the mechanisms of A12 (the one-line answer to a call) and A16 (an attack call refused inside the room) rewritten in model/arrows.jsonl, the stage C2 sentences kept as mechanism_C2 and mechanism_fails_if_C2, mechanism_source from-literature, work named, mechanism_test recording the C3b read. A call is the first part of a pair; joining is the preferred answer and comes bare, declining is dispreferred and comes with a reason, and in a refusal of an attack call the reason states the room's norm or the attack's cost. The failure clauses gain the mechanism's own observation (joins as reasoned as refusals, or refusals as bare as joins). Strength, counts and instances unchanged; A12 stays theorised (never counted), tested on attack calls only. history.jsonl 85 lines. Snapped C3-move-relating-50.
